Figure 3:WeVisForensics and its training strategy, DTPO.The investigator rolls out with a fixed FSL snapshot and is updated on every batch with outcome rewards and CLUE. Grounded calls (𝒟OPD\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{OPD}}) queue by role in the interaction pool, from which the slow process distills privileged EMA teachers into students, revises skill cards, and refreshes the FSL everyHHsteps.

Figure 4:Overview of ForenCue-30K.Curated videos are annotated with role-specific artifact evidence and converted into sub-agent records and interaction trajectories, and an RL pool supports DTPO. Examples show artifacts targeted by each sub-agent.

Figure 5:Self-evolution of the forensic library over training.(a)Sub-agent verdicts on training calls, scored against role-level annotations. Left: moving averages of the miss rate on generated videos and of the verdict F1 over LoRA refreshes (minor ticks). Middle: role-level error per sub-agent across the early, middle, and late phases of training. Right: evidence F1 of the frozen library and of the evolved library at the early, middle, and final checkpoints on four test benchmarks, each spanning the appearance, physical, and OCR axes clockwise.(b)Accepted edits, with oneReportand oneIgnorerule each. The gray card shows candidate rules that failed the acceptance test.(c)Three generated test videos inspected by the three checkpoints, with verbatim sub-agent excerpts and the agent’s final answer.

Figure 6:Qualitative comparison on a generated video with warping handwritten text.Left:a)The CoT-based VideoVeritas[36]dismisses the garbled text as stylistic without inspecting it.b)In the fixed-workflow ARGUS[56], texture, lighting, and motion reports outweigh the detected text deformation.Right:The SFT or DTPO-trained main agent paired with the SFT or evolved sub-agents. The evolved sub-agents flag the glyph anomalies, and only the trained main agent, which moves its OCR inspection to the warped text at 7 s, turns them into a fake verdict.

Figure 12:Comparison of AI-generated video detection paradigms.a) CoT-based reasoning uses textual rationales. b) Multi-agent workflows follow fixed execution structures. c) WeVisForensics adaptively coordinates sub-agents and evolves them together with the main policy.

Figure 13:Qualitative comparison of investigation paradigms.All three approaches classify the generated video as fake. The CoT-based detector makes unsupported motion claims, and the fixed-workflow detector aggregates predefined observer reports. The adaptive agent requests localized appearance and OCR inspections and grounds its verdict in changing emblem contours and degraded apron lettering.

Figure 14:Complete evolution comparison.On an AI-generated video, the CoT-based VideoVeritas and the fixed-workflow ARGUS both answer real. Before DTPO (top right), the appearance sub-agent reports no issue and WeVisForensics answers real. After DTPO (bottom right), the same first inspection localizes soft hand and finger boundaries during the opening gesture, and the main agent answers fake.
